lead: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pushes out in one minute. Doctors need it to judge whether a sick heart is pumping enough, and to guide drugs and fluids. Dilution methods measure it without opening the chest: inject a known amount of indicator into the blood, then record how the indicator concentration changes downstream. The faster the blood flows, the more the indicator is spread out and the smaller the concentration peak becomes. This chapter covers two hospital standards: dye dilution with indocyanine green, and thermal dilution with cold saline through a pulmonary artery catheter.
prereq: You need: the cardiac cycle and the transducer and bio-amplifier basics; the pressure measurement in 2.1 shows the same idea of a sensor on a catheter.

sections.h3: Cardiac output and the dilution principle

blocks.text: Cardiac output (CO) is the blood volume the heart ejects per minute, in litres per minute (L/min). At rest an adult heart moves about 5 L/min; during exercise it can rise several times. CO = heart rate × stroke volume, but measuring stroke volume directly is hard, so dilution methods infer the flow from how blood carries an injected indicator.

The Fick principle is the reference method: oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference gives CO. It needs blood oxygen measurement (see Blood gas analyzers and pH measurement). Dilution methods use the same conservation idea with an indicator instead of oxygen.

Inject a known mass I (mg) of indicator into a vein. Downstream, a sensor records concentration c(t) in mg/L against time t in seconds. If blood flow is Q in L/s and the indicator mixes completely, then I = Q ∫ c(t) dt. The integral A = ∫ c(t) dt has units mg·s/L and is the area under the concentration-time curve. Rearranged and converted to minutes:

blocks.where: CO is cardiac output in L/min; I is the mass of indicator injected in mg; A = ∫ c(t) dt is the area under the first-pass concentration-time curve in mg·s/L; 60 converts seconds to minutes.

blocks.text: The method assumes complete mixing, no indicator loss before the sensor, and steady flow during the measurement. Those assumptions are the reason the recording technique matters.

Dye dilution uses indocyanine green (ICG), a green dye that stays in the blood vessels and is removed by the liver. A typical dose is 5 mg, injected rapidly into a central vein. Arterial blood is drawn through a densitometer, a small cuvette that measures light absorption at the dye's wavelength. The recorder plots dye concentration against time. The curve starts to rise a few seconds after injection, when the first bolus reaches the sampling site, peaks a few seconds later, then falls.

After about 20–30 s some dye returns through the circulation and creates a second, smaller hump called recirculation. That hump is not part of the first pass. To find the true first-pass area, plot the falling part of the curve on semilog paper, fit a straight line, and extend it below the recirculation hump. The area under the first-pass curve — the measured part plus the extrapolated part — is A. Because the extrapolated part is an exponential, its area is simply the concentration where extrapolation starts multiplied by the time constant τ of the decay.
Some ICG preparations contain sodium iodide, so ask about iodine allergy. The method is accurate when the curve is clean. The area is what matters; the height alone is not CO.

sections.h3: Thermal dilution and the Swan-Ganz catheter

blocks.text: Thermal dilution replaces the dye with cold fluid and the densitometer with a thermistor. A Swan-Ganz catheter floats through the right heart into the pulmonary artery. It has a proximal port in the right atrium and a thermistor near its tip in the pulmonary artery. A known volume, commonly 10 mL, of cold saline or dextrose is injected into the right atrium. The thermistor records the small fall and recovery of blood temperature as the cold bolus passes.
The recorder plots the temperature fall ΔT (°C) against time (s). The area under this curve, A<sub>T</sub> = ∫ ΔT dt, has units °C·s. Heat takes the place of the dye mass in the dilution equation:

blocks.where: CO is cardiac output in L/min; V<sub>I</sub> is the injectate volume in litres; T<sub>B</sub> and T<sub>I</sub> are the blood and injectate temperatures in °C; K<sub>1</sub> = (density × specific heat of injectate) ÷ (density × specific heat of blood), about 1.08 for 5 % dextrose; A<sub>T</sub> is in °C·s; 60 converts L/s to L/min.

blocks.text: Monitors fold everything except A<sub>T</sub> into one computation constant K, so CO = K / A<sub>T</sub>; the constant also corrects for the warming of the injectate inside the catheter. Enter the K for the injectate volume and temperature actually used: a wrong K gives a wrong CO even when the curve is perfect.

Iced injectate (0–4 °C) gives a larger temperature difference from blood and so a better signal-to-noise ratio; room-temperature injectate is easier to handle but needs its own constant. Thermal dilution needs no dye and can be repeated every few minutes; its risks are those of the catheter itself.

figure.caption: The worked example's samples every 2 s (dots) give area A₁ by trapezoids up to 16 s; the dashed decay, continued under the recirculation hump, adds A₂. The shaded first-pass area of 61.3 mg·s/L gives 4.9 L/min.

examples.question: 5 mg of indocyanine green is injected. The arterial densitometer gives these concentrations (mg/L) every 2 s from 4 s to 16 s: 0, 3.0, 7.5, 6.0, 4.2, 3.0, 2.1. After 16 s recirculation lifts the curve. (a) Find the first-pass area, extrapolating the decay beyond 16 s. (b) Find the cardiac output. (c) What would an operator get by also counting a recirculation area of 20 mg·s/L?
steps: The tail falls from 3.0 to 2.1 mg/L in 2 s, a ratio of 0.70, so on semilog paper it is a straight line with time constant τ = 2 / ln(3.0/2.1) = 2 / 0.357 = 5.61 s.
Area under the extrapolated tail from 16 s on: A₂ = c(16) × τ = 2.1 × 5.61 = 11.8 mg·s/L.
First-pass area A = A₁ + A₂ = 49.5 + 11.8 = 61.3 mg·s/L.
(b) CO = 60 I / A = 60 × 5 / 61.3 = 4.90 L/min. Units: mg ÷ (mg·s/L) = L/s, times 60 s/min gives L/min.
(c) With the recirculation area added, A = 81.3 mg·s/L and CO = 300 / 81.3 = 3.69 L/min, about 25 % too low.
examples.answer: A = 61.3 mg·s/L and CO = 4.9 L/min; counting recirculation would wrongly give 3.7 L/min.

examples.question: 10 mL of 5 % dextrose at 2 °C is injected into the right atrium of a patient whose blood is at 37 °C. The thermistor curve has area A<sub>T</sub> = 4.5 °C·s. Take K<sub>1</sub> = 1.08. (a) Find the cardiac output. (b) The next injection uses injectate at 22 °C. What area should the curve have if the output is unchanged, and why is iced injectate preferred?
steps: (b) Now T<sub>B</sub> − T<sub>I</sub> = 37 − 22 = 15 °C. For the same CO, A<sub>T</sub> = 60 × 0.010 × 15 × 1.08 / 5.04 = 1.93 °C·s.

The area falls in the ratio 15/35 = 0.43, so the curve is less than half as tall while the noise from breathing and blood temperature drift stays the same. Iced injectate gives the better signal-to-noise ratio.
examples.answer: CO = 5.0 L/min; with 22 °C injectate the area would be only 1.93 °C·s, so iced injectate gives a cleaner reading.

traps: Dropping the factor 60 in CO = 60 I / A. With I = 5 mg and A = 60 mg·s/L, dropping 60 gives 0.083 L/s (not L/min), which is the same as 5 L/min.
Including the recirculation hump in A. That makes A too large and CO too small, because CO is inversely proportional to the area.
Mixing time units: the area must be in mg·s/L before multiplying by 60. If the curve is integrated in mg·min/L, do not multiply by 60 again.
Using the wrong computation constant K for thermal dilution when the injectate volume or temperature is changed. The curve can be correct while CO is wrong.

quiz.q: Define cardiac output and give a typical resting value for an adult.
quiz.a: Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart ejects per minute, in L/min. A typical resting adult value is about 5 L/min.

quiz.q: Which indicator is used in dye dilution, and what sensor measures it in the arterial line?
quiz.a: Indocyanine green is used, and a densitometer measures its light absorption in arterial blood.

quiz.q: Why is the downslope of the dye curve extrapolated before the area is measured?
quiz.a: The downslope is extrapolated to remove the recirculation hump. Otherwise the second pass of dye would be counted in A, making A too large and the calculated CO too small.

quiz.q: Why does iced injectate improve the thermal dilution signal?
quiz.a: Iced injectate gives a larger temperature difference between injectate and blood, so the thermistor sees a larger ΔT. The signal is bigger compared with baseline noise.

quiz.q: A patient has cardiac output 4 L/min and 5 mg of dye is injected. What first-pass area would the dye curve give?
quiz.a: Rearrange CO = 60 I / A to A = 60 I / CO = 60 × 5 / 4 = 75 mg·s/L.

quiz.q: A thermal dilution measurement uses 5 mL of injectate, but the monitor's computation constant K is set for 10 mL. The temperature-time curve is valid. What does the monitor report?
quiz.a: The monitor computes CO = K / A<sub>T</sub>. K is proportional to V<sub>I</sub>, so the constant for 10 mL is twice the right one for 5 mL, and the monitor reports about twice the true CO. The curve A<sub>T</sub> itself is valid; the operator must enter the K for 5 mL.

beyond: Not for the exam. Intensive care units now often estimate cardiac output from arterial pulse contour analysis, calibrated by transpulmonary thermodilution or lithium dilution, and echocardiography gives a non-invasive estimate. Search for "pulse contour cardiac output" and "transpulmonary thermodilution". Some syllabi list the blood cell counter beside this topic; it is taught with the clinical laboratory instruments.
